title: Berber vs Plush vs Frieze Carpet: Which Style Fits Your Home?
meta: Berber, plush or frieze carpet? Plush for bedrooms, frieze for family rooms and stairs, Berber for offices. Wills Flooring installs all three, $0.99 / sq ft.
keywords: berber vs plush carpet, frieze carpet pros and cons, best carpet style for bedrooms, berber carpet with pets, carpet styles explained, carpet installation Edmonds WA

blocks.lead: Plush is the right pick for bedrooms and formal rooms, frieze wins in busy family rooms and on stairs, and Berber makes sense in offices and low-traffic rooms as long as nobody in the house has claws.
blocks.detail: The three names describe how the yarn is cut and twisted, not how good the carpet is. Labor is the same whichever you pick: $0.99 per sq ft to stretch in over pad and $30 per stair, so what moves your price is the carpet and pad, not the style name.

blocks.html: The question usually arrives at our Lynnwood showroom as "I like the soft one but my sister says Berber lasts longer, which is right?" Both are half right. Edmonds makes the choice interesting because so many homes are 1950s to 1970s ramblers in Seaview and Westgate with three small bedrooms off one hallway, a family room down a short flight of stairs, and a living room used twice a year. Those rooms want different carpet. Here is what each style is, where it holds up, and how to combine them.

blocks.text: What the three styles actually are

items.title: Plush (also called Saxony or velvet)
items.text: Yarn is cut at the top and lightly twisted, so the surface is smooth and dense. It feels the softest underfoot and looks the most formal. The trade-off: the yarn tips lie down when you walk on them, so plush shows footprints, vacuum lines and traffic lanes more than any other style.

items.title: Frieze (twist or textured)
items.text: Same cut yarn, but twisted hard, five to seven turns per inch, and heat-set so the strands curl and kink. The kinked surface hides footprints, dirt and vacuum marks and springs back after traffic. Short-strand textured frieze is the default family-room carpet in new homes for a reason.

items.title: Berber
items.text: The yarn is not cut at all. It loops back into the backing, which makes a tight, flecked, hard-wearing surface that hides dirt well and holds up in commercial hallways. Its weakness is the loop: a cat claw, dog nail or chair caster can catch one loop and pull a run across the room.

blocks.note: Ratings assume the same fiber and the same pad. Fiber choice (nylon, triexta, polyester, wool) changes durability more than style does.

blocks.text: Room by room in an Edmonds house

items.html: Bedrooms and formal rooms: plush. A bedroom sees bare feet, not boots, so the softest option is also the sensible one. Retirees downsizing into the Bowl condos almost always choose plush for the master, and a light plush in the front room is what buyers expect in an older Edmonds home.

Family room off the kitchen: frieze. In the Seaview and Perrinville split-levels the lower family room takes the dog, the kids and the popcorn. A textured frieze in a mid-tone flecked color hides all three.

Stairs: short frieze, or a small-loop Berber if there are no pets. Stairs wear on the nosing, where the carpet bends over the edge. Plush shows that bend wear first. Long shaggy frieze wraps badly around the nose and looks sloppy within a year.
Home office: Berber or a dense low plush. Berber takes a rolling chair better than any cut pile, and a chair mat solves the snag risk. If a cat shares the office, switch to a low, dense plush.

Daylight basement: Berber or frieze in a synthetic fiber. Many Westgate and Esperance homes have basement rooms a few feet below grade. Skip wool and thick plush there; humidity near the water is real, and a synthetic pile on a moisture-barrier pad vacuums clean.

blocks.text: Mixing styles in one house without it looking pieced together

items.title: Keep one color family
items.text: Plush in the bedrooms and frieze in the family room look intentional when both are the same warm gray or the same oatmeal. Two different beiges from two different mills is what looks like a patch job.

items.title: Change style at a doorway, never mid-hall
items.text: A transition under a closed door is invisible; one mid-hallway is a seam everyone sees. Carpet the hall in whichever style the stairs get, and switch inside the bedroom doors. Keep the two pile heights within about 1/4 in so you do not feel a step.

blocks.title: The Berber and pets rule:
blocks.text: We get called to repair snagged Berber more than any other carpet problem. One pulled loop can be re-tucked. A run that unravels across a room cannot, and the only fix is a patch that never quite matches. With a cat or a big dog, choose a cut pile.
How to choose the right one at your kitchen table

items.html: Bend the sample backwards. If you can see the backing through the pile, the carpet is too thin for the room, whichever style it is.
Look at the sample in your own light. Edmonds gray-sky daylight is bluer than showroom light, and a carpet that looked warm under fluorescent bulbs can go cold in a north-facing Seaview bedroom.

Pair the pad to the style. Plush wants a dense 8 lb rebond to stay springy; Berber wants a firmer, thinner pad so the loops do not flex and pop; stairs want the firmest pad you can get. See our guide to carpet padding in Edmonds.

Ask what the warranty excludes. Most texture-retention warranties exclude stairs and some exclude Berber snags. A 1-year workmanship warranty from Wills Flooring covers the installation itself, seams and stretch.

faq.q: Is Berber carpet more durable than plush?
faq.a: With the same fiber, a loop pile resists crushing better than a cut pile, so Berber holds its look longer in a hallway. But Berber has a failure mode plush does not: snagged loops that run. With pets or rolling chairs in the house, a dense frieze or plush usually outlasts it.

faq.q: Which carpet style is best for stairs?
faq.a: A short, dense frieze or a small-loop Berber. Stairs wear where the carpet bends over the nosing, and a tight pile survives that bend. Avoid long shaggy frieze and thick soft plush on stairs; both look matted on the nose within a year or two of daily use.

The long, shaggy 1970s style frieze does. The modern version is a short, tightly twisted cut pile that reads as a clean, slightly flecked surface. It is the most common carpet in new Snohomish County construction today, and it hides footprints better than anything else on the market.

faq.q: Can I put plush carpet in a family room?
faq.a: You can, but pick a dense, heavy plush in a mid-tone and accept the vacuum lines and footprints. If the room has a dog, kids and a couch used every night, a frieze in the same color will look better after three years, for the same labor rate and roughly the same material cost.

faq.q: Is Berber carpet bad for cats?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. A cat that scratches at carpet catches loops and pulls them, and one pulled loop can unravel a visible line across the room. Cut pile styles like plush and frieze have no loops to catch. If you love the Berber look, a cut-and-loop pattern is a safer compromise.

faq.q: Does the carpet style change the installation price?
faq.a: No. Wills Flooring stretches in plush, frieze or Berber for the same $0.99 per sq ft in labor, $1.29 glue-down, $30 per stair, on a 500 sq ft minimum. What moves your bill is the carpet and pad, which we quote with samples at your Edmonds home, about 10 minutes from the Lynnwood showroom.
